1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.background: Named after the Welsh sea captain William Davies Evans, the first player known to have played it, in a game against McDonnell in London in 1827. William Lewis published the first analysis in 1832, and the gambit became extremely popular.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4.strategy: Takes the pawn and accepts the challenge. Black is a pawn up, and White's compensation is time: the bishop on b4 is hit again after c3, so White builds a broad centre with tempo and a lead in development. Black's task is to find the moment to give the pawn back and defuse the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.background: Aron Nimzowitsch defended declining the gambit in My System, arguing that it loses no tempo because b4 does nothing for development anyway. Most commentators nevertheless judge declining weaker than accepting the pawn and returning it later.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.strategy: Declines the pawn and keeps the bishop on its diagonal, so White cannot gain time with c3. But the move wastes a tempo, and White's b-pawn has gained space on the queenside, which gives White the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 d5.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Hein Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 d5.strategy: Strikes back in the centre at once, attacking both the bishop and the e4 pawn. After 5.exd5 the knight on c6 is attacked, but 5...Nxb4 saves it and removes the pawn that hits the bishop on c5. A sharp, offbeat reply that leaves White the choice.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 b5.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Fontaine Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 b5.strategy: Hits the bishop with a pawn, but neither capture hurts White: after 5.Bxb5 Bxb4 the pawns are merely traded, and the bishop on b5 now attacks the knight that guards e5. Black has opened its own queenside and gets nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.strategy: Threatens a5, after which the bishop on b6 has no safe square: the a7 pawn blocks its retreat and the b4 pawn covers c5. Black must make room at once, and White keeps a lasting space advantage on the queenside.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.B.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined, Cordel Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.B.strategy: Brings the bishop to the long diagonal, so that e5 is attacked a second time and has only the knight to defend it. A natural, developing move, but it does not threaten the bishop on b6 the way a4 does.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Chases the knight in the hope of winning e5, but ...Na5 hits the bishop with tempo and the pawn on b5 has little to do. Sound, since White loses nothing, but the attack is premature and Black is comfortable.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.strategy: Makes room for the bishop: without it, a5 would trap the piece on b6. The a-pawn move is the useful one here, keeping the bishop on its diagonal and the centre intact, and Black accepts a modest space deficit on the queenside.
Clears a7 for the bishop just as ...a6 does, but it leaves b5 free for White: the pawn can advance with tempo against the knight on c6, and Black has made no developing move.
Develops and hits e4 but ignores the threat: 6.a5 attacks the bishop on b6, and with the a7 pawn still in place every square the bishop can reach loses material. The pawn move has to come first.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined, Showalter Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.strategy: Develops the knight toward d5, using the queenside space the pawns have gained. White keeps a small but lasting edge, which comes from that extra space.

Supports the b4 pawn and prepares d4, aiming for a broad pawn centre. It takes c3 from the queen's knight, so it gives up the quicker development of the main move and is the more modest way to use the space.
Gets the king safe before the centre opens. A sound, unhurried move, but it adds nothing to the queenside space plan and leaves Black free to choose the set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Saves the knight and attacks the bishop on c4 in the same move. The cost is that e5 loses its defender, so White can win a pawn, but Black gets active play in return and White's king is still in the centre.
Offers a trade of knights and sets a trap: 6.Nxe5? runs into ...Qg5 with a strong attack. White does better to take on d4, after which Black recaptures and the pawn on b5 has gained little.

Gives up the e5 pawn: with the knight gone from c6 nothing guards it, so 6.Nxe5 wins it at once, and the knight and the bishop on c4 both eye f7. Black is under pressure with nothing to show for the pawn.

Takes the unguarded pawn, defends the bishop and eyes f7 in one move. The knight on e5 is loose and White's king is still in the centre, so Black gets counterplay with the queen against the knight and g2. It is the only move that wins the pawn, so White has to defend accurately.
Retreats the bishop out of the knight's reach and keeps the threat against e5, but gives Black a free move to defend the pawn or develop, so the pawn advance has cost White a tempo.

Offers the bishop for the knight that has strayed to the rim. After ...Nxb3 axb3 White has doubled b-pawns and has given up the bishop pair, but the a-file is half-open for the rook and e5 is still under attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined, Hirschbach Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Hits the loose knight on e5 and the g2 pawn at once, while the bishop on b6 points at f2 and the knight on a5 still eyes the bishop on c4. White has more to answer than one move can cover, and Black takes the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined, Lange Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Guards f7, the point both the knight and the bishop aim at, and develops a piece. The knight on a5 keeps pressing the bishop. Less forcing than a queen sortie, but it leaves Black well placed after White's premature pawn advance.
Trades the stranded knight for the bishop at once, but 7.Nxc4 recaptures with a gain of time against the bishop on b6 and White keeps a clean extra pawn. Black has nothing to show for the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Hits the bishop again and prepares to build a centre with d4, so the bishop must move for a second time. This is the point of the gambit: White gives a pawn for time and a pawn centre, and the queen also gets the b3 square, aiming at f7 together with the bishop.
Castles and leaves the bishop on b4 alone, so Black gets a free move to consolidate and White's compensation is development only. Without a quick pawn centre, the gambit pawn is hard to justify.

Develops the bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at e5, but does not attack Black's bishop on b4. Black loses no time and keeps the pawn, so White has paid a pawn for development alone and has little to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Main Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: The main retreat: the bishop stays on the diagonal to e1, so once White plays d4 the c3 pawn is pinned and cannot simply recapture. It keeps the pawn and sets the sharpest test of the gambit, but takes a5 away from the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Anderssen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: The safest retreat: the bishop cannot be hit again soon, covers g5 and helps the king, and leaves a5 free for the knight to challenge the bishop on c4. Black often returns the pawn later and aims for a solid, balanced game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Stone-Ware Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..background: Named after Henry Nathan Stone and Preston Ware. Grandmasters including Andrei Volokitin, Alexander Grischuk and Loek van Wely have played it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Adds a defender to e5, so that d4 no longer arrives with an attack on the pawn. The price is that the bishop blocks the d-pawn. A solid, less trodden way to keep the extra pawn for now.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, McDonnell Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Goes back to the square it came from in the hope of stopping d4, but White plays it anyway with tempo on the bishop. The position stays sound for Black, yet three bishop moves for one pawn give White a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Mayet Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Undevelops the bishop completely: Black has spent three moves to win a pawn with it and, to castle, must bring it out again as well as the g8 knight. Sound, since the pawn stays, but White takes the centre with a large lead in development.

Strikes in the centre at once: the pawn attacks e5, and White aims for a full pawn centre backed by the lead in development. Black must choose between keeping the pawns and giving some back, while White is often happy to offer a second pawn for the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Slow Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..background: Popular in the Romantic era, it is now a notable but much rarer alternative to 6.d4.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Castles first, so that the c3 pawn is not pinned against the king when d4 comes. Safe and sensible, but slow: Black gets time to consolidate and to return the pawn under good conditions, which takes much of the sting out of the gambit.

A sideline that lines up the queen and bishop against f7, which only the king guards, so Black must spend a move on defence. White gains time, but the queen is committed early and the central strike is put off.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Bronstein Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: The solid reply: a pawn protects e5, d7 opens for the queen and the bishop on c8 gets the diagonal to g4. Black keeps the extra pawn without grabbing a second one, though White's lead in development still brings attacking chances.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Pierce Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Takes the pawn and keeps both extra pawns for the moment: cxd4 is impossible because the bishop on a5 pins the c3 pawn to the king. But White does not need to hurry, and quick development brings strong attacking chances, so Black has to defend precisely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Leonhardt Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Offers the b-pawn: if the bishop takes, ...Nxd4 attacks it and the f3 knight while the pinned c3 pawn cannot recapture. The play is level, but a gambit within a gambit asks Black to find sharp moves, so it ranks below the main replies.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Laroche Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Counterattacks e4 but ignores the centre. White takes on e5 with tempo on the knight, and the natural capture on e4 runs into a queen move to d5, which attacks the knight and threatens mate on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Protects e5 with a pawn, frees the queen's bishop and keeps the extra pawn. It leads to much the same structures as the main line, with White having spent a move on castling instead of a central advance.
Develops with an attack on e4, which White cannot simply leave: it forces White to act in the centre at once. Black keeps the pawn and prepares to castle, and the game takes its own course.

Develops the knight to a square from which it supports a ...d5 break against the bishop on c4, while the bishop on a5 stays on its diagonal. Black keeps the extra pawn, but the knight does not hit e4, so White is free to build the centre.
Gains another tempo on the bishop: the pawn attacks both c5 and e5 and builds the centre. Black's retreat to c5 did not stop it, and the bishop must move once more.

Castles first and keeps the central strike in hand, since the bishop on c5 stays exposed to it. Sound, but it gives Black a move to find a better square for the bishop, and the gambit's tempo gain is lost.

Lines up queen and bishop against f7, but Black defends it at once, with ...Qf6 or ...Qe7, and keeps the extra pawn. White has delayed the central strike that gains a tempo on the bishop and has little to show for it.
Takes the pawn and with it removes the attacker of the bishop. Black is a pawn up and White's compensation lies in the open lines and strong central pawns that come after recapturing.

Retreats out of reach of the pawn and keeps the bishop on the diagonal that eyes f2, but e5 is not held: White trades on e5 and wins the pawn back, with a small edge for White and a cramped game for Black.

Defends e5 with the bishop and keeps the extra pawn for now, but it blocks the d-pawn and leaves the queen's bishop shut in. Black has spent a fourth move on the bishop, so White's lead in development gives it a clear initiative.

The usual follow-up to c3: the pawn takes the centre and attacks e5. The bishop on e7 cannot be hit by it, so White gains no tempo here, but the centre is big and Black must find a safe way to return the extra pawn.

Brings the queen out with a battery on f7. The bishop on e7 shuts the queen's route to its defence, so Black must defend or allow Bxf7+. White still gets the centre afterwards, but the early queen move is a sideline that delays the central strike.
Castles first and keeps the central strike for later. Black's bishop is already safe on e7, so waiting gains no tempo, and Black gets time to consolidate and return the pawn on good terms.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Anderssen Variation, Cordel Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Attacks the bishop on c4 at once, the move that the retreat to e7 made possible since a5 is free for the knight. Black gains time to challenge the centre and, if need be, to hand the pawn back for a solid game.
Takes the pawn at once and keeps the extra pawn for the moment. White recaptures with a broad centre, and Black must find a way to challenge it or hand the pawn back on good terms.
Defends e5 with a pawn and frees the queen's bishop, keeping the extra pawn. It is solid, but it leaves the centre to White, who keeps the space and the freer game.
